title: NRI Deposits Drop 23% as Diaspora Savers Shift to Dollar Accounts
excerpt: Fresh deposit inflows from non-resident Indians fell to $2.78 billion in the April-June quarter, with a 93% plunge in rupee accounts offset by a doubling of foreign-currency deposits following RBI intervention.
body:
• Fresh NRI deposit inflows fell 23% year-over-year to $2.78 billion in April-June 2026, according to RBI data
  • FCNR(B) foreign-currency deposits more than doubled to $1.73 billion, while rupee-denominated NRE inflows plunged 93%
  • Total outstanding NRI deposits remained nearly flat at $168.5 billion, masking a significant shift from rupee to dollar accounts
  • The RBI's special FCNR(B) swap window, set to close August 31, has drawn $72.8 billion in total forex inflows since June

Fresh deposits by non-resident Indians into Indian banks dropped 23% year-over-year to $2.78 billion during the April-June quarter, even as a sharp shift toward dollar-denominated accounts reshaped the composition of NRI savings, Reserve Bank of India data released this week showed.

The decline, from $3.61 billion in the same period last year, was driven almost entirely by a collapse in rupee-denominated deposits. Inflows into NRE (non-resident external) accounts fell 93% to just $140 million, while NRO (non-resident ordinary) account deposits came in at $900 million.

Dollar Deposits Surge

The one bright spot was foreign currency non-resident deposits, known as FCNR(B), which more than doubled to $1.73 billion from $774 million a year earlier — a 124% jump. The surge came after the RBI introduced a special forex-swap facility in June, under which the central bank agreed to bear the cost of currency hedging to encourage dollar inflows into India.

"FCNR deposits being foreign-currency denominated, do not carry currency risk, and the surge suggests that NRIs are increasingly choosing to deposit savings in this instrument rather than rupee-denominated deposits."

— The Hindu BusinessLine

The shift suggests NRIs are responding rationally to currency risk. With the rupee under pressure and the dollar strengthening, parking money in foreign-currency accounts eliminates exchange-rate exposure — a key consideration for diaspora savers sending money to India.

Outstanding Deposits Flat

Despite the drop in fresh inflows, the total stock of NRI deposits edged up marginally to $168.5 billion at end-June 2026, from $168.3 billion a year earlier. Outstanding FCNR(B) deposits rose 5.7% to $35.5 billion, while NRE deposits declined 3.8% to $98.8 billion. NRO deposits stood at $34.3 billion.

The near-flat outstanding balance indicates that while NRIs are depositing less new money, they are not withdrawing existing funds at significant rates.

RBI's Dollar Window Draws $72.8 Billion

The RBI's special FCNR(B) facility, launched during the June monetary policy meeting, has proved far more effective than traditional deposit channels. As of August 21, the facility had attracted total forex inflows of $72.85 billion, with FCNR(B) deposits accounting for $65.4 billion of the total, according to authorized dealer bank data reported by the central bank.

However, the RBI announced on August 14 that it will close the special swap window for fresh FCNR(B) deposits on August 31 — one month ahead of the originally scheduled September 30 deadline. The early closure suggests the central bank has met its near-term forex accumulation targets.

Why NRI Deposits Are Slowing

The broader decline in NRI deposits extends a pattern seen over the past year. Fresh inflows fell 16% across the first nine months of FY26, and dropped 40% in the first half, according to earlier RBI data. Analysts have pointed to several factors behind the trend.

A narrowing interest rate differential between India and the United States has reduced the incentive for NRIs to park money in Indian accounts. Some estimates suggest NRIs are channeling more capital into Indian equity markets rather than fixed deposits, according to Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist at Bank of Baroda.

Madhavi Arora, Chief Economist at Emkay Global Financial Services, has noted that falling interest differentials, combined with the income effects of slowing Western economies, will continue to shape NRI deposit flows.

What It Means for NRIs

For Indian Americans and other diaspora communities maintaining financial ties to India, the data underscores a shifting calculus. Dollar-denominated FCNR(B) deposits offer protection from rupee depreciation but typically carry lower interest rates than NRE accounts. The RBI's willingness to subsidize hedging costs through the special window made FCNR(B) deposits temporarily more attractive — but with that window closing August 31, the incentive structure is set to change again.
